title: Population Pyramids, Demographic Transition and Dependency Ratios

steps.title: Reading a pyramid in ten seconds
steps.tx: A **population pyramid** stacks percent of males (left) and females (right) by 5-year age groups, youngest at base. Shape is diagnosis: broad base with rapid taper means high fertility and mortality (expansive), straight sides mean stationary replacement, and a bulging middle with narrow base means constrictive ageing. India's pyramid is bottom-heavy but its base has begun shrinking.
steps.say: Base first, then taper. Broad and narrowing fast: expansive youth. Straight sides: stationary. Bulging middle, pinched base: ageing. India's base stays broad yet has begun to shrink, the transition made visible.

steps.title: Demographic transition in five stages
steps.tx: The **demographic transition** walks from high stationary (birth and death both high) through early expanding (deaths fall first), late expanding (births fall), low stationary (both low), to declining (births below deaths). India sits in late expanding nationally with southern states ahead. Deaths always fall first; that lag is the population explosion's entire mechanism.
steps.say: Deaths fall first; births follow late. That lag through expanding stages is the explosion's whole mechanism. India stands late-expanding nationally, southern states a stage ahead. Five stages, one ordering rule.

steps.title: Dependency ratio: workers carrying non-workers
steps.tx: The **dependency ratio** divides dependents (0 to 14 plus 65 and above) by the working age population (15 to 64), times 100. Young dependency dominates India's ratio today; old-age dependency climbs as transition proceeds. The ratio prices schools versus pensions in budgets more honestly than total population ever does.
steps.say: Dependents over workers, times one hundred. India's burden is young today and ages steadily. Budgets price schools against pensions from this ratio, never from raw population totals.

steps.title: Demographic dividend: the window
steps.tx: The **demographic dividend** opens when working-age share bulges while dependency falls, offering accelerated growth if jobs, skills and health meet the cohort. It is a window, not an entitlement: unemployed bulges convert dividend into unrest in the cautionary literature. India's window spans roughly the mid-2000s to mid-2050s in common projections, peaking state by state at different decades.
steps.say: A bulge can pay or explode. Workers swelling while dependents shrink offers growth only where jobs, skills and health meet them. India's window runs decades wide, peaking state by state on different clocks.

steps.title: Sex ratio and its distortions
steps.tx: **Sex ratio** (females per 1000 males in Indian convention) reads 943 in Census 2011 nationally while child sex ratio (0 to 6 years) fell to 919, accusing sex selection despite overall improvement; NFHS rounds report ratios at birth separately. Kerala's favourable ratios against northern deficits map development and son preference simultaneously on one indicator.
steps.say: Females per thousand males: nine forty three overall in 2011, child ratio nine nineteen and falling then. One indicator maps development and son preference simultaneously, state by state.

steps.title: Life expectancy and the mortality transition
steps.tx: **Life expectancy** at birth rose in India from about 32 years in 1951 to 69.4 in recent programme ledgers, 37 years added across the family welfare era, while crude death rate fell from 23 to about 6. Epidemiologic transition rides alongside: infections recede, non-communicable and injury shares climb, and dual burden defines the middle passage India occupies.
steps.say: Thirty two to sixty nine years across seven decades; death rates quartered. Infections recede while chronic disease and injuries climb, the dual burden of the middle passage India now occupies.

steps.title: Stable, stationary and growing populations
steps.tx: A **stationary population** has birth equal to death with no migration (zero growth), a stable population grows at constant rate with fixed structure, and exponential doubling time follows the rule of 70 divided by growth percent. Census decadal growth fell from 21.54 (2001) to 17.64 percent (2011) in the ledger, deceleration examiners quote as transition evidence.
steps.say: Vocabulary closes the set. Stationary means births equal deaths; stable means constant growth structure; doubling follows seventy over growth percent. Decadal growth decelerating across censuses evidences transition.

points: Decadal growth still decelerating in India

steps.title: Migration bends pyramids locally
steps.tx: **Migration** carves pyramids at working ages: male out-migration hollows origin districts' young adult bars (feminised villages, remittance economies) while destination cities bulge with young men. Census place-of-birth and last-residence streams quantify it. Local health planning ignoring migration misjudges denominators for immunisation, maternity and NCD registers alike.
steps.say: Migration carves the middle bars. Origin villages feminise and age; destination cities bulge young and male. Denominators ignoring movement corrupt every register from immunisation to NCD follow-up.

steps.title: From pyramid to service planning
steps.tx: **Planning reads pyramids forward**: today's 0 to 4 bar is the school cohort in 5 years and the reproductive cohort in 20; today's bulge is tomorrow's hypertension register. Facility norms per population silently assume structures; ageing districts need chronic care where young districts need maternity beds, from the same norm rupees.
steps.say: Read bars as future queues. Toddlers become school cohorts, then parents, then hypertension registers. Ageing districts buy chronic care with the same norm rupees young districts spend on maternity beds.
